transitivity: both — transitive (perform a song), intransitive (perform on stage)
gloss: To present music, a play, or a dance in front of an audience.
examples: They *perform* twice every Saturday.
She *performed* the whole piece from memory.
The quartet has *performed* in nineteen countries.

transitivity: both — transitive (act the part of a king), intransitive (act in a film)
gloss: To play a part in a play, film, or television show.
examples: He wants to *act*, not direct.
She *acted* in commercials before her first movie.
He has been *acting* since the age of six.

transitivity: both — transitive (play the cello), intransitive (the band played for an hour)
gloss: To make music on an instrument, or to perform a piece of music.
examples: She *plays* the cello beautifully.
The band *played* for three hours without a break.
That song has been *played* on every station in town.
contrast: With an instrument English keeps *the*: *play the piano*. With a style it drops the article: *play jazz*.

transitivity: both — transitive (dance a waltz), intransitive (dance all night)
gloss: To move your body in time with music.
examples: They *dance* every Friday at the community hall.
She *danced* the lead in Swan Lake.
He has been *dancing* since he could walk.
contrast: American /dæns/ with the vowel of *cat*, not British /dɑːns/.

transitivity: both — transitive (rehearse a scene), intransitive (rehearse all week)
gloss: To practice a play, concert, or dance before performing it publicly.
examples: We *rehearse* every evening this week.
They *rehearsed* the fight scene twenty times.
The cast is *rehearsing* on the real set now.

transitivity: both — transitive (practice scales), intransitive (practice for an hour)
gloss: To do something again and again in order to get better at it.
examples: She *practices* scales for an hour every morning.
He *practiced* the solo until his fingers hurt.
They have been *practicing* all month for the recital.
contrast: American spells the noun and the verb alike, *practice*; British uses *practise* for the verb.

transitivity: both — transitive (audition forty dancers), intransitive (audition for a part)
gloss: To try out for a part in a performance, or to hear someone try out.
examples: Two hundred singers *audition* here every year.
She *auditioned* for the lead and got it.
He is *auditioning* dancers all afternoon.
contrast: A performer *auditions for* a part; a director *auditions* the performers.

transitivity: both — transitive (improvise a solo), intransitive (improvise for ten minutes)
gloss: To make up music, words, or action as you go, without preparing it.
examples: Good actors can *improvise* when a line is dropped.
The pianist *improvised* for ten minutes.
They were *improvising* the entire second half.

gloss: To learn something so well that you can repeat it without looking.
examples: Opera singers *memorize* the whole score.
She *memorized* her lines in two days.
He has *memorized* every word of the play.
contrast: American *memorize*; British usually *memorise*.

transitivity: both — transitive (recite a poem), intransitive (recite from memory)
gloss: To say a poem or passage aloud from memory.
examples: Each child will *recite* one poem.
He *recited* the opening speech perfectly.
The same blessing is *recited* at every meal.

gloss: To tell a story aloud, or to speak the voice-over of a film.
examples: A famous actor will *narrate* the documentary.
She *narrated* the audiobook herself.
The film is *narrated* by the youngest brother.

transitivity: both — transitive (mime opening a door), intransitive (mime on the sidewalk)
gloss: To act something out using only movement, with no words.
examples: Street performers *mime* for the tourists.
He *mimed* opening a very heavy door.
The singer was obviously *miming* the words.

gloss: To copy someone's voice and manner, for comedy or to fool people.
examples: He can *impersonate* every president since Nixon.
She *impersonated* the director so well that we all laughed.
That comedian has been *impersonating* him for years.

gloss: To copy the way someone speaks, moves, or works.
examples: Young painters often *imitate* their teachers.
The parrot *imitated* the doorbell.
His early songs were clearly *imitating* Dylan.

gloss: To copy someone's voice or gestures, often to make fun of them.
examples: He can *mimic* any accent in the room.
She *mimicked* her brother's walk all the way home.
The synthesizer is *mimicking* a cello.
contrast: A *k* is inserted before the ending: *mimicked*, *mimicking* — like *panic → panicked*.

gloss: To perform or explain a work in your own way.
examples: Every pianist *interprets* the sonata differently.
She *interpreted* the role as a comedy.
The poem has been *interpreted* a dozen ways.

gloss: To act out a scene or an event.
examples: The children *enact* the whole story with puppets.
The company *enacted* the battle on the town green.
The old legend is *enacted* every summer.

gloss: To act out a past event again, in detail.
examples: Volunteers *reenact* the battle every July.
They *reenacted* the scene for the documentary.
The arrest was *reenacted* on television.
contrast: Written *reenact* in American English; the spelling *re-enact* is also seen.

gloss: To turn a story into a play or film, or to make something sound more exciting than it was.
examples: They plan to *dramatize* the novel for radio.
The papers *dramatized* a simple disagreement.
Her life has been *dramatized* twice already.
contrast: American *dramatize*; British usually *dramatise*.

transitivity: both — transitive (pose the models by the window), intransitive (pose for a portrait)
gloss: To hold a position so that someone can paint, draw, or photograph you.
examples: Students *pose* for each other in the drawing class.
She *posed* for the same painter for ten years.
The family is *posing* by the fountain.
contrast: You *pose for* a photographer or a painter.

gloss: To bend forward from the waist to thank an audience.
examples: The cast *bows* three times on a good night.
She *bowed* and the applause doubled.
They were still *bowing* when the curtain came down.
contrast: To bend forward is /baʊ/, rhyming with *now*. The *bow* you play a violin with, and the *bow* in a ribbon, are /boʊ/.

gloss: To bend the knees and lower the body slightly as a formal greeting or thank-you.
examples: The ballerinas *curtsy* at the end of every performance.
She *curtsied* to the audience and ran off.
The little dancers have been *curtsying* all evening.
contrast: Consonant + y, so it becomes *curtsies* and *curtsied*, but the y stays in *curtsying*.

transitivity: both — transitive (applaud the soloist), intransitive (the crowd applauded)
gloss: To clap your hands to show that you liked a performance.
examples: Some audiences *applaud* between movements.
They *applauded* for a full five minutes.
She was *applauded* before she even sang a note.

transitivity: both — transitive (boo the villain), intransitive (the crowd booed)
gloss: To shout in disapproval at a performer or a performance.
examples: A few fans always *boo* the villain.
The crowd *booed* when the band left after forty minutes.
He has never been *booed* off a stage.
contrast: The double o stays and the ending is simply added: *booed*, *booing*.

transitivity: both — transitive (juggle five oranges), intransitive (juggle for the crowd)
gloss: To keep several objects moving through the air by throwing and catching them.
examples: Clowns *juggle* while the stage is reset.
He *juggled* five oranges without dropping one.
She is *juggling* torches now.

gloss: To move your hand or head in order to express something.
examples: Actors *gesture* more broadly on a large stage.
He *gestured* toward the empty chair.
She was *gesturing* wildly from the wings.
contrast: You *gesture to* or *gesture toward* someone or something.

gloss: To lead people to their seats or through a door.
examples: Students *usher* at the Friday concerts.
An attendant *ushered* us up to the balcony.
The late guests were *ushered* in through a side door.

gloss: To tell an audience who or what is coming next.
examples: The host will *introduce* each act.
She *introduced* the band in Spanish and English.
The piece was *introduced* by the composer himself.

gloss: To signal a performer or a technician to begin.
examples: The conductor will *cue* the horns at bar forty.
He *cued* the lights a second too early.
The choir is waiting to be *cued*.
contrast: Both *cuing* and *cueing* are correct; American writing prefers *cuing*.

ru: играть главную роль; снимать в главной роли
transitivity: both — transitive (the film stars her), intransitive (star in a comedy)
gloss: To play the leading part in a film or show.
examples: She *stars* in the new comedy.
He *starred* opposite his own daughter.
The play is *starring* a complete unknown.
contrast: The r doubles before an ending: *starred*, *starring*. An actor *stars in* a film.

transitivity: both — transitive (direct a film), intransitive (he writes and directs)
gloss: To be in charge of how a film, play, or piece of music is performed.
examples: She *directs* two shows a season.
He *directed* the whole film in nineteen days.
The opera is being *directed* by a newcomer.

gloss: To put on a play or a public event.
examples: The company *stages* a new musical every fall.
They *staged* Hamlet in a parking garage.
The whole argument was *staged* for the cameras.

transitivity: both — transitive (the theater premiered her play), intransitive (the ballet premieres in October)
gloss: To show or perform something publicly for the very first time.
examples: The ballet *premieres* in October.
The film *premiered* at a small festival in Texas.
Her symphony has already *premiered* in Chicago.

transitivity: both — transitive (debut a new song), intransitive (she debuted at twenty)
gloss: To appear or be presented in public for the first time.
examples: Three young singers *debut* with the orchestra this season.
The show *debuted* to excellent reviews.
They are *debuting* two new songs tonight.
contrast: The t is silent: /deɪˈbjuː/, day-BYOO — but it is heard again in *debuted*, day-BYOOD.

transitivity: both — transitive (headline the festival), intransitive (two bands headline on Saturday)
gloss: To be the main act at a concert or festival.
examples: Two bands *headline* on Saturday night.
She *headlined* the festival at twenty-three.
They are *headlining* three nights in a row.

gloss: To work together with someone on a creative project.
examples: The two composers *collaborate* constantly.
She *collaborated* with a choreographer from Havana.
They have *collaborated* on four albums.
contrast: You *collaborate with* a person and *collaborate on* a project.

transitivity: both — transitive (chant her name), intransitive (the monks chant at dawn)
gloss: To sing or say the same words over and over on one or two notes.
examples: The monks *chant* at dawn.
The crowd *chanted* her name for five minutes.
The same two lines are *chanted* throughout the piece.

transitivity: both — transitive (harmonize a melody), intransitive (the sisters harmonize)
gloss: To sing or play notes that fit pleasingly with a melody.
examples: The sisters *harmonize* without even trying.
He *harmonized* a third below the melody.
They have been *harmonizing* together since childhood.
contrast: American *harmonize*; British usually *harmonise*.

transitivity: both — transitive (conduct the Ninth), intransitive (she conducts from the piano)
gloss: To lead an orchestra or choir with your hands or a baton.
examples: She *conducts* from the piano.
He *conducted* the Ninth Symphony from memory.
The concert was *conducted* by a guest from Vienna.
contrast: The verb is stressed kuhn-DUKT; the noun *conduct*, meaning behavior, is KAHN-dukt.

gloss: To arrange music for an orchestra, or to organize something carefully.
examples: He *orchestrates* his own film scores.
She *orchestrated* the song for forty players.
The whole evening had been carefully *orchestrated*.

transitivity: both — transitive (strum a guitar), intransitive (strum quietly)
gloss: To play a guitar by sweeping your fingers across the strings.
examples: He *strums* quietly while she sings.
She *strummed* the same four chords all night.
Someone was *strumming* on the porch.
contrast: The m doubles: *strummed*, *strumming*.

gloss: To pull a string with your fingers to make a note.
examples: Harpists *pluck* with both hands.
She *plucked* the low string once and stopped.
The violins are *plucked* in this passage.

transitivity: both — transitive (drum a rhythm), intransitive (drum for a band)
gloss: To beat a drum, or to tap out a rhythm.
examples: He *drums* for two different bands.
She *drummed* on the table with a pencil.
Rain was *drumming* on the roof of the tent.
contrast: The m doubles: *drummed*, *drumming*.

transitivity: both — transitive (tune a guitar), intransitive (the orchestra is tuning)
gloss: To adjust an instrument so that it plays at the right pitch.
examples: Guitarists *tune* between almost every song.
He *tuned* the piano the morning of the recital.
The whole orchestra is *tuning* now.
contrast: American /tuːn/, TOON; British says /tjuːn/, TYOON.

gloss: To move a piece of music into a different key.
examples: Singers often ask you to *transpose* a song down.
She *transposed* the aria for a lower voice.
The whole number has been *transposed* into G.

gloss: To make a new version of a recording by rearranging its parts.
examples: Producers *remix* almost every hit now.
He *remixed* the single for the clubs.
The track has been *remixed* four times.
contrast: Ends in *-x*, so the third person adds *-es*: *remixes*.

gloss: To learn something completely, or to prepare the final version of a recording.
examples: It takes years to *master* the violin.
She *mastered* the piece in under a month.
The album was *mastered* in Nashville.

transitivity: both — transitive (rap a verse), intransitive (rap over a beat)
gloss: To speak rhyming words in rhythm over a beat.
examples: He *raps* in two languages.
She *rapped* the last verse alone.
They have been *rapping* together since high school.
contrast: The p doubles: *rapped*, *rapping*. Sounds exactly like *wrapped*.

transitivity: both — transitive (croon a ballad), intransitive (croon into the microphone)
gloss: To sing softly and sweetly, usually a love song.
examples: He *croons* old standards on Sunday nights.
She *crooned* the baby back to sleep.
A voice was *crooning* from the radio in the kitchen.

gloss: To sing or play music for someone, especially outdoors.
examples: Strolling musicians *serenade* the diners.
He *serenaded* her from the sidewalk below.
We were *serenaded* through the entire meal.

transitivity: both — transitive (blare music all night), intransitive (a trumpet blared)
gloss: To make a loud, harsh sound.
examples: The speakers *blare* until midnight.
A trumpet *blared* from the balcony.
Music was *blaring* in the next apartment.

transitivity: both — transitive (sync the audio to the video), intransitive (the dancers sync perfectly)
gloss: To make sound and picture, or two performers, match exactly in time.
examples: The dancers *sync* perfectly with the beat.
He *synced* the audio to the video overnight.
Her lips are not *synced* with the track.
contrast: Sounds exactly like *sink*. The longer spelling *synch* exists, but *sync* is the usual American form.

gloss: To play or sing alone while the rest of the group stays quiet or accompanies.
examples: The saxophone *solos* after the second chorus.
She *soloed* for a full three minutes.
He was *soloing* with his eyes closed.
contrast: The final o stays and *-ed* is added: *soloed*, not *solod*.

transitivity: both — transitive (rhyme moon with June), intransitive (those two lines rhyme)
gloss: To end with the same sound as another word or line.
examples: Those two lines don't quite *rhyme*.
He *rhymed* every couplet in the song.
She has been *rhyming* words since she was four.
contrast: Silent h after the r, and a silent final e: *rhyme*, *rhymed*.

transitivity: both — transitive (vary the tempo), intransitive (prices vary)
gloss: To change something a little from one time to the next, or to be different from one case to another.
examples: Try to *vary* the tempo in the second verse.
She *varied* the pattern in every panel.
Ticket prices have *varied* wildly this season.
contrast: Consonant + y, so it becomes *varies* and *varied*, but the y stays in *varying*.

transitivity: both — transitive (waltz her around the room), intransitive (waltz until midnight)
gloss: To dance a waltz, a smooth dance in three-beat time.
examples: The couples *waltz* slowly around the floor.
They *waltzed* until the band packed up.
She is *waltzing* with her grandfather.
contrast: Ends in *-tz*, so the third person adds *-es*: *waltzes*.

transitivity: both — transitive (twirl a baton), intransitive (twirl across the stage)
gloss: To spin around quickly, or to spin something with your fingers.
examples: Little girls *twirl* whenever they get a new dress.
She *twirled* under his arm and back again.
He was *twirling* a drumstick between his fingers.

transitivity: both — transitive (the wind swayed the branches), intransitive (sway to the music)
gloss: To move slowly from side to side.
examples: The whole crowd *sways* during that song.
She *swayed* in time with the music.
They were *swaying* with their arms around each other.

transitivity: both — transitive (stomp the floor), intransitive (stomp in time)
gloss: To put your feet down hard and loudly.
examples: The dancers *stomp* on every downbeat.
He *stomped* off the stage in the middle of a song.
They were *stomping* so hard the floor shook.

transitivity: both — transitive (strut the runway), intransitive (strut across the stage)
gloss: To walk proudly, with your chest out, so that people look at you.
examples: Models *strut* the length of the runway.
He *strutted* across the stage in a gold jacket.
She was *strutting* like she owned the place.
contrast: The t doubles: *strutted*, *strutting*.

transitivity: both — transitive (whirl a partner around), intransitive (whirl in circles)
gloss: To turn around very fast.
examples: The dancers *whirl* until the music stops.
She *whirled* around to face the audience.
Skirts were *whirling* all over the floor.

ru: двигаться в ритм, ловить кайф от музыки
gloss: To move easily and happily with the rhythm of music.
examples: The whole room *grooves* when he plays.
We *grooved* to old soul records all night.
The bass player was *grooving* with his eyes shut.
contrast: You *groove to* the music.

gloss: To design the steps and movements of a dance.
examples: She *choreographs* for two companies at once.
He *choreographed* the fight scenes as a dance.
The number was *choreographed* in a single afternoon.
contrast: The *ch* is /k/ and the *ph* is /f/: KOR-ee-uh-graf.

transitivity: both — transitive (parade the costumes), intransitive (parade down Main Street)
gloss: To walk in a public procession, or to show something off in public.
examples: The bands *parade* down Main Street every June.
The winners *paraded* through the town.
The costumes were *paraded* in front of the judges.

transitivity: both — transitive (doodle a face), intransitive (doodle in a notebook)
gloss: To draw simple, absent-minded pictures while your mind is on something else.
examples: I always *doodle* during long meetings.
She *doodled* little stars all over the margin.
He was *doodling* on the back of the menu.

transitivity: both — transitive (scribble a note), intransitive (scribble on the wall)
gloss: To write or draw quickly and carelessly.
examples: Please don't *scribble* on the walls.
He *scribbled* an address on a napkin.
She has *scribbled* notes in every margin of the book.

gloss: To darken part of a drawing so that it looks solid or rounded.
examples: *Shade* the left side of the apple so it looks round.
She *shaded* the background with a soft pencil.
The face still looks flat because you haven't *shaded* it.

transitivity: both — transitive (color the sky blue), intransitive (the kids color for an hour)
gloss: To put color onto a drawing or a surface.
examples: The kids *color* for an hour every afternoon.
He *colored* the sky with three shades of blue.
She is *coloring* inside the lines now.
contrast: American *color, colored, coloring*; British *colour, coloured, colouring*.

gloss: To give something a light shade of color.
examples: One drop of red will *tint* a whole jar of white paint.
The photographer *tinted* the old print a warm brown.
The windows have been *tinted* to cut the glare.

gloss: To draw the pictures that go with a text.
examples: She *illustrates* children's books for a living.
A local artist *illustrated* the whole series.
The poem has been *illustrated* in ink and watercolor.

gloss: To show someone or something in a picture, film, or story.
examples: The mural *depicts* the founding of the city.
Goya *depicted* the horrors of war.
The king is *depicted* on horseback.

gloss: To represent a person or thing in art, or to play a character.
examples: The film *portrays* him as a quiet hero.
She *portrayed* Juliet at nineteen.
He has *portrayed* the same detective for ten seasons.
contrast: Vowel + y, so the y stays: *portrayed*, not *portraid*.

gloss: To draw, paint, or perform something in a particular way.
examples: Few painters *render* light the way he does.
The architect *rendered* the facade in soft gray.
The aria was beautifully *rendered*.

gloss: To cut a design into metal or glass with acid or a sharp tool.
examples: They *etch* the design onto a copper plate.
He *etched* his initials into the glass.
The scene is *etched* in fine, dark lines.
contrast: Ends in *-ch*, so the third person adds *-es*: *etches*.

gloss: To paint a shape or letters through a cut-out sheet.
examples: They *stencil* the numbers onto every seat.
She *stenciled* vines along the top of the wall.
The name was *stenciled* on the case in white.
contrast: American *stenciled, stenciling* with one l; British *stencilled, stencilling*.

gloss: To cut off the edges of a picture or photograph.
examples: *Crop* the photo so the lamp isn't in the corner.
He *cropped* the image down to a square.
The poster has been badly *cropped*.
contrast: One vowel plus one consonant, so the p doubles: *cropped*, *cropping*.

gloss: To make small changes to a photograph or painting to improve it.
examples: Magazines *retouch* almost every cover.
The lab *retouched* the scratches out of the negative.
That portrait has clearly been *retouched*.

transitivity: both — transitive (photograph a wedding), intransitive (she photographs well)
gloss: To take a picture of someone or something with a camera.
examples: He *photographs* birds at dawn.
They *photographed* the whole ceremony.
The painting has never been properly *photographed*.
contrast: The verb keeps the stress on the first syllable, FOH-tuh-graf; *photography* moves it: fuh-TAH-gruh-fee.

gloss: To make a camera picture larger or smaller without moving the camera.
examples: Don't *zoom* in the middle of a shot.
The camera *zoomed* slowly onto her face.
He was *zooming* out to show the whole hall.
contrast: Almost always with *in* or *out*: *zoom in on a face*, *zoom out*.

transitivity: both — transitive (exhibit twenty canvases), intransitive (she exhibits in Paris)
gloss: To show work publicly in a gallery or museum.
examples: Three local painters *exhibit* here every spring.
She *exhibited* in Paris for the first time last year.
His drawings are being *exhibited* downtown.
contrast: The h is silent and the x sounds like /ɡz/: ig-ZIB-it.

gloss: To choose and organize the works in a show or a collection.
examples: She *curates* the museum's photography wing.
A student *curated* the entire exhibit.
The playlist was *curated* by the band itself.

gloss: To show a new work publicly for the first time.
examples: They *unveil* the statue on Saturday.
The gallery *unveiled* three new pieces last night.
The mural was *unveiled* to loud applause.

transitivity: both — transitive (sign a program), intransitive (she signs for an hour after each show)
gloss: To write your name on something, especially a work of art or an autograph.
examples: Artists usually *sign* the bottom right corner.
She *signed* forty programs after the show.
The print is numbered and *signed*.
contrast: The g is silent: /saɪn/, SYN. It comes back in *signature*, SIG-nuh-chur.

gloss: To put a short line of text under a picture or across a screen.
examples: Newspapers *caption* every photograph.
He *captioned* the picture 'Last day of summer.'
All the videos are *captioned* in two languages.

gloss: To make drawings or models appear to move in a film.
examples: They *animate* every frame by hand.
A small studio *animated* the opening credits.
The characters were *animated* in clay.

transitivity: both — transitive (embroider a shirt), intransitive (she embroiders every evening)
gloss: To sew a decorative design onto cloth.
examples: She *embroiders* flowers on everything she owns.
His grandmother *embroidered* all the pillowcases.
The costume is *embroidered* with gold thread.

transitivity: both — transitive (quilt a blanket), intransitive (they quilt on Thursdays)
gloss: To sew layers of cloth together into a padded cover or pattern.
examples: The women *quilt* together every Thursday.
She *quilted* a blanket for the new baby.
The jacket is *quilted* across the shoulders.

gloss: To arrange or design something so that it looks a particular way.
examples: She *styles* the sets for a fashion magazine.
They *styled* the shoot after a 1970s album cover.
The whole room was *styled* by the director herself.

gloss: To form a picture of something in your mind.
examples: Close your eyes and *imagine* the stage completely empty.
He *imagined* the whole opera before writing a note.
She had never *imagined* performing for so many people.
contrast: Followed by *-ing*, not by *to*: *imagine living there*, not *imagine to live there*.

gloss: To show a feeling or an idea through art, words, or movement.
examples: Dancers *express* emotion with the whole body.
The painting *expressed* his grief better than any letter.
She has *expressed* the same theme in every song.
contrast: Ends in *-ss*, so the third person adds *-es*: *expresses*.

gloss: To stand for an idea in a work of art.
examples: The broken chain *symbolizes* freedom.
For the poet, winter *symbolized* old age.
Doves have long *symbolized* peace.
contrast: American *symbolize*; British usually *symbolise*.

gloss: To make one part stand out, in a picture or in a performance.
examples: A little white paint will *highlight* the cheekbone.
The review *highlighted* her second solo.
The dancer's hands are *highlighted* by a single spot.

gloss: To present something in a way that shows its best qualities.
examples: The festival *showcases* young composers.
The recital *showcased* her whole range.
Three student films are being *showcased* tonight.

ru: показывать, включать (в состав); выступать в главной роли
gloss: To include someone or something as an important part of a show or work.
examples: The album *features* a children's choir.
The show *featured* a guest violinist.
She has been *featured* on three magazine covers.

transitivity: both — transitive (project a film onto the wall), intransitive (learn to project)
gloss: To throw an image onto a screen, or to make your voice carry to the back of a hall.
examples: Singers learn to *project* without shouting.
They *projected* old home movies onto the back wall.
Her voice has always *projected* well.
contrast: The verb is stressed on the second syllable, pruh-JEKT; the noun *project* is PRAH-jekt.

gloss: To write the words for a film, play, or show.
examples: Two writers *script* every episode.
He *scripted* the documentary in a single week.
The whole argument was *scripted*.

transitivity: both — transitive (film a scene), intransitive (they film all summer)
gloss: To record something with a movie camera.
examples: They *film* the rehearsals for the archive.
She *filmed* the whole ceremony on her phone.
The scene was *filmed* at four in the morning.

gloss: To cut and arrange film, sound, or text into its final form.
examples: He *edits* all his own videos.
She *edited* three hours down to ninety minutes.
The album is still being *edited*.

gloss: To replace the speech in a film with another language, or to add sound to it.
examples: Studios *dub* most cartoons into Russian.
They *dubbed* the film into six languages.
The laughter was *dubbed* in later.
contrast: The b doubles: *dubbed*, *dubbing*.

gloss: To speak the lines of a character in an animated film, or to say an opinion aloud.
examples: She *voices* three characters in the same cartoon.
He *voiced* the villain in both sequels.
The dragon is *voiced* by a famous actor.

gloss: To broadcast something on television.
examples: They *televise* the awards live every year.
The network *televised* the final concert.
Opening night was *televised* around the world.

transitivity: both — transitive (stream a concert), intransitive (the song is streaming everywhere)
gloss: To send or watch video or music over the internet as it plays.
examples: Thousands *stream* the show every night.
The band *streamed* the whole concert for free.
Her new single is *streaming* everywhere.

gloss: To show or see something before its official release.
examples: The gallery *previews* the show for members.
Critics *previewed* the film on Monday.
Two songs have already been *previewed* online.

gloss: To make something widely known to the public.
examples: They barely *publicize* the smaller concerts.
The theater *publicized* the opening for months.
The tour has been heavily *publicized*.
contrast: American *publicize*; British *publicise*.

gloss: To discuss the strengths and weaknesses of a piece of work.
examples: Students *critique* each other's drawings every Friday.
The teacher *critiqued* my phrasing, not my technique.
Every scene was *critiqued* line by line.
contrast: The *-que* is /k/: kri-TEEK, rhyming with *week*.

gloss: To say publicly that someone or something is very good.
examples: Critics rarely *praise* a first novel this loudly.
They *praised* her timing and her voice.
The production has been *praised* everywhere.
contrast: You *praise someone for* something: *they praised her for her timing*.

transitivity: both — transitive (judge a competition), intransitive (she judges every year)
gloss: To decide the quality of something, or who has won a competition.
examples: Three musicians *judge* the final round.
She *judged* the piano competition last spring.
The entries are *judged* without names attached.

gloss: To say how good something is, often by giving it a score.
examples: Viewers *rate* every episode online.
The reviewer *rated* the concert four stars.
The film is *rated* very highly by critics.

gloss: To officially suggest someone for a prize or a position.
examples: The academy *nominates* five films a year.
They *nominated* her for best director.
He has been *nominated* three times and never won.
contrast: You *nominate someone for* an award.

gloss: To show great public respect for someone.
examples: The festival *honors* a living composer each year.
They *honored* him with a lifetime award.
She was *honored* at a dinner in New York.
contrast: The h is silent: AH-nur. American *honor, honored*; British *honour, honoured*.

gloss: To hold someone's attention so completely that they cannot look away.
examples: Her voice *mesmerizes* a room in about four bars.
The dancer *mesmerized* the whole theater.
The children sat *mesmerized* through the puppet show.
contrast: American *mesmerize*; British usually *mesmerise*.

gloss: To delight someone completely, as if by magic.
examples: Simple melodies *enchant* small children.
The production *enchanted* even the hardest critics.
We were *enchanted* by the costumes.

gloss: To feel great surprise and admiration at something.
examples: Visitors still *marvel* at the ceiling.
She *marveled* at how quickly he learned the part.
They stood *marveling* at the size of the canvas.
contrast: You *marvel at* something. American *marveled, marveling* with one l; British *marvelled, marvelling*.

transitivity: both — transitive (repeat the chorus), intransitive (the pattern repeats)
gloss: To do or say something again.
examples: *Repeat* the last four bars, please.
She *repeated* the chorus twice more.
The pattern is *repeated* across the whole canvas.

gloss: To play a recording again.
examples: They *replay* the best moments at the end of the show.
He *replayed* the take a dozen times.
The scene was *replayed* in slow motion.
contrast: The verb is stressed ree-PLAY; the noun *replay* is REE-play.

gloss: To make a copy of a picture, a sound, or a piece of work.
examples: Cheap printing cannot *reproduce* those colors.
The museum *reproduced* the fresco at full size.
The drawing has been *reproduced* on posters and mugs.

gloss: To make something as good as it can possibly be.
examples: Dancers spend years *perfecting* a single turn.
He *perfected* the trick before showing anyone.
She has *perfected* that accent.
contrast: The verb is stressed pur-FEKT; the adjective *perfect* is PUR-fikt.

gloss: To present an idea for a film, show, or project, hoping someone will pay for it.
examples: Writers *pitch* dozens of shows a year.
She *pitched* the series to three studios in one week.
The idea was *pitched* as a one-hour drama.
contrast: Ends in *-ch*, so the third person adds *-es*: *pitches*.

transitivity: both — transitive (exaggerate a gesture), intransitive (he always exaggerates)
gloss: To make something seem bigger, better, or worse than it really is.
examples: Stage actors *exaggerate* their gestures a little.
He *exaggerated* every movement for comic effect.
The features are deliberately *exaggerated* in the caricature.
contrast: Double g, and the x sounds like /ɡz/: ig-ZAJ-uh-rayt.
